## Exercises  {#Exercises_DataReshaping}

Many of the exercises below build and solidify our data wrangling skills that rely on the use of operations taught in Chapter 4 and Chapter 7. This is a great time to review those chapters if you have not been using the syntax frequently. The exercises below have been written in a way that YOU must do all the data wrangling yourself - the time for providing lots of code to help you over the hump is over - your data science wrangling skills start now!
    
### Exercise 1 {-}

A common task is to take a set of data that has multiple categorical variables and create a table of the number of cases for each combination. An introductory statistics textbook contains a data set summarizing student surveys from several sections of an intro class. The two variables of interest are `Gender` and `Year` which are the students gender and year in college. *Note: you will need to refer to Chapter 4 and Chapter 7 for some of the operations needed below - this is a great time to review chapter 4!*

**a)** Download the data set using the following:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
Survey <- read.csv('https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets2e/StudentSurvey.csv', na.strings=c('',' ')) #na.strings - makes missing cells trurn na in the dataframe
```

I downloaded the Survey dataset using read.csv

**b)** Select the specific columns of interest **Year** and **Gender**

```{r}
Survey_YG <- Survey %>%
  select(Year, Gender)
```
I used the select function to select the columns Year and Gender

**c)** Convert the **Year** column to factors and properly order the factors based on common US progression (FirstYear - Sophomore - Junior - Senior)
```{r}
Survey_YG <- Survey_YG %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(Year)) #Makes the Year column a factor

#factors are just an additional layer to the data give - they assign numbers to categorical varaibles but don't necessarily change the actual data 

Survey_YG <- Survey_YG %>%
  mutate(Year = fct_relevel(Year, 'FirstYear', 'Sophomore', 'Junior', 'Senior')) #manually leveling the factors to be in correct First year - senior order
```
I mutated the Year column into a factor, and then releveled them so that the correct order would be FirstYear', 'Sophomore', 'Junior', 'Senior'

**d)** Convert the **Gender** column to factors and rename them Male/Female.

```{r}
Survey_YG <- Survey_YG %>%
  mutate(Gender = factor(Gender))

Survey_YG <- Survey_YG %>%
  mutate( Gender = fct_recode(Gender, 'Male'   = 'M'),
          Gender = fct_recode(Gender, 'Female'   = 'F') )
#Could also use if else here, but fct_recode works as well
#fct_recode (desired column new factor name, old factor name)
```
I mutated the Gender column into a factor and then recoded Male to be M and Female to be F

**e)** Produce a data set with eight rows and three columns that contains the number of responses for each gender:year combination. *You might want to look at the following functions: `dplyr::count` and `dplyr::drop_na`.*

```{r}
Survey_YG_new <- count(Survey_YG, Gender, Year) %>% drop_na(Year)
#count(dataframe, column, column - automatically groups stuff + counts the responses)
```
Using the `dplyr::count` I counted the responses by gender and year and then used `dplyr::drop_na` to drop the NA's in the Year column

**f)** Pivot the table in part (e) to produce a table of the number of responses in the following form:
        
|   Gender    |  First Year  |  Sophomore  |  Junior   |  Senior   |
|:-----------:|:------------:|:----------:|:---------:|:---------:|
|  **Female** |              |            |           |           |  
|  **Male**   |              |            |           |           | 

```{r}
Survey_YG_wide <- Survey_YG_new %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = n) #pivot at whatever 'column' you want to becoe column names 

Survey_YG_wide
```
The original dataset was long, so I used pivot wide to pivot on Year and use the values from n to make a wider table. 

### Exercise 3 {-} 

For this problem we will consider two simple data sets.

```{r, eval=TRUE}
A <- tribble(
  ~Name, ~Car,
  'Alice', 'Ford F150',
  'Bob',   'Tesla Model III',
  'Charlie', 'VW Bug')

B <- tribble(
  ~First.Name, ~Pet,
  'Bob',  'Cat',
  'Charlie', 'Dog',
  'Alice', 'Rabbit')
```

**a)** Combine the data frames together to generate a data set with three rows and three columns using `join` commands. 

```{r}
#B <- B %>%
#rename(Name = First.Name) #This was an optional renaming step so that I could join with column names being the same but can do that in the full_join command using join_by - also another way to do it later

ABjoined <- full_join(A,B, join_by(Name== First.Name))
```
I originally renamed the column First.Name in B to Name and then joined, but discovered an easier way using join_by (Name == First.Name).

**b)** It turns out that Alice also has a pet guinea pig. Add another row to the `B` data set. Do this using either the base function `rbind`, or either of the `dplyr` functions `add_row` or `bind_rows`.

```{r}

B <- B %>%
  add_row(First.Name = 'Alice', Pet = 'Guinea Pig') #Litearally just used add_row to add a row

```
I added a row to the B dataframe to show that Alice also owned a Guinea Pig.

**c)** Combine again the `A` and `B` data sets together to generate a data set with four rows and three columns using `join` commands.

```{r}
ABjoined2 <- left_join(A,B, join_by(Name== First.Name))
```
I repeated the same process I did above in a to rejoin the A and B with the updated information about Alice. I used left join so that Ford F150 would be in the column "Car" for Alice instead of an NA

*Note: You may want to also try using `cbind` to address questions (a) and (c). Leave this as a challenge question and focus on the easier to use `join` functions introduced in this chapter.*

### Exercise 4 {-} 

The package `nycflights13` contains information about all the flights that arrived in or left from New York City in 2013. This package contains five data tables, but there are three data tables we will work with. The data table `flights` gives information about a particular flight, `airports` gives information about a particular airport, and `airlines` gives information about each airline. Create a table of all the flights on February 14th by Virgin America that has columns for the carrier, destination, departure time, and flight duration. Join this table with the airports information for the destination. Notice that because the column for the destination airport code doesn't match up between `flights` and `airports`, you'll have to use the `by=c("TableA.Col"="TableB.Col")` argument where you insert the correct names for `TableA.Col` and `TableB.Col`.

```{r}
NYCdates_carrier <- flights %>% #This filters the whole dataset for what I want/ the day/month and carrier specified in the problem so that I dont have to worry about extra radnom data that is not applicable 
  filter(month == 2, day == 14) %>%
  filter(carrier == 'VX')

Feb14thVXflights <- left_join(NYCdates_carrier, airports, by = c("dest" = "faa")) 
#found that dest == faa in practicality but were named different things, so used by( vecotr of the title that havbe the same information but different names)

head(Feb14thVXflights)

Feb14thVXflights.trim <- Feb14thVXflights %>%
  select(year, month, day, carrier, dest, dep_time, air_time)
#optional extra step - just firther selected the specified columns stated in the problem
Feb14thVXflights.trim
```
I cleaned the orginal data frame "flights" and filtered by date (month and day) and then by carrier (Virgin Airlines, which in the airlines dataset ahad a code for VX.) I then used left_join to join my cleaned flights dataframe (Feb14thVXflights) with airports by *"by = c("dest" = "faa")"*. I then did an extra step to just select the columns of interest stated in the problem and made a new dataframe (Feb14thVXflights.trim).
